details:
**"Because I could not stop for Death"**
Dickinson's most famous poem and the most common giveaway. Death "kindly stopped for me," and the speaker rides in a carriage that "held but just Ourselves - / And Immortality," passing a school, "Fields of Gazing Grain," and the "Setting Sun - / Or rather - He passed us," before pausing at "a House that seemed / A Swelling of the Ground" (her grave); it ends with the realization that "the Horses' Heads / Were toward Eternity."

**"I heard a Fly buzz - when I died"**
A poem narrated by a speaker at the moment of her death. There is "Stillness in the Room" like the "Stillness in the Air - / Between the Heaves of Storm," she has "Signed away / What portion of me be / Assignable," and then a fly with a "Blue - uncertain - stumbling Buzz" comes between her and the light until "I could not see to see."

**"'Hope' is the thing with feathers"**
A poem describing hope as a little bird "That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all." The speaker has "heard it in the chillest land - / And on the strangest Sea," yet it "never, in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of Me."

**"I felt a Funeral, in my Brain"**
A poem describing a mental breakdown as a funeral inside the speaker's head. "Mourners to and fro" keep treading, "A Service, like a Drum - / Kept beating - beating - till I thought / My Mind was going numb," mourners in "Boots of Lead" creak across her soul, and finally "a Plank in Reason, broke." In a related poem, Dickinson wrote that "The Brain - is wider than the Sky."

**"I'm Nobody! Who are you?"**
A short poem in which the speaker happily declares herself a "Nobody" and asks if the reader is one too. She remarks "How dreary - to be - Somebody!", comparing public fame to being a frog that tells its name all day "To an admiring Bog."

**"Wild Nights - Wild Nights!"**
A short, famously sensual love poem. The speaker says that "Futile - the Winds - / To a Heart in port - / Done with the Compass - / Done with the Chart!", imagines "Rowing in Eden," and longs, "Might I but moor - tonight - / In Thee!"

**"Success is counted sweetest"**
One of the few poems published in Dickinson's lifetime, arguing that "Success is counted sweetest / By those who ne'er succeed" and that "To comprehend a nectar / Requires sorest need." It ends with a dying soldier of the defeated side hearing the "distant strains of triumph" of the "purple Host" that won.

**Thomas Wentworth Higginson**
The writer and editor who became Dickinson's longtime correspondent and literary mentor. She first wrote to him in 1862 after reading his Atlantic article "Letter to a Young Contributor," asking whether her "Verse is alive"; he recorded her saying that she knew something was poetry if she felt "physically as if the top of my head were taken off," and he co-edited her poems after her death.

**The "Master" letters and "My Life had stood - a Loaded Gun"**
Three draft letters addressed to an unidentified "Master," found after her death and possibly never sent. "Master" also appears in the poem "My Life had stood - a Loaded Gun," in which the speaker's gun belongs to a mysterious "Owner" and which ends "For I have but the power to kill, / Without - the power to die."

**"Safe in their Alabaster Chambers"**
A poem about the dead lying in their tombs, "Untouched by Morning - / And untouched by Noon," as "the meek members of the Resurrection." Dickinson revised its second stanza several times, in one version writing that "Diadems - drop - and Doges - surrender - / Soundless as dots - on a Disc of Snow."

**"Much Madness is divinest Sense"**
A poem arguing that the majority decides what counts as sanity. If you "Assent - and you are sane," but "Demur - you're straightway dangerous - / And handled with a Chain."

**"A narrow Fellow in the Grass"**
A poem about encountering a snake, which parts the grass "as with a Comb." The speaker has felt friendly toward many creatures, but never met this fellow "Without a tighter breathing / And Zero at the Bone."

**"I taste a liquor never brewed"**
A poem in which the speaker becomes drunk on nature itself, drinking "From Tankards scooped in Pearl" a liquor "Not all the Frankfort Berries / Yield such an Alcohol!" She calls herself an "Inebriate of air" and a "Debauchee of Dew."

**The "Belle of Amherst," her dashes, and Susan Gilbert**
Dickinson lived reclusively in Amherst, Massachusetts, and is known for her heavy use of dashes, slant rhyme, and capitalized nouns; William Luce's one-woman play The Belle of Amherst is about her. Her closest correspondent was her sister-in-law Susan Gilbert Dickinson, and their letters are collected in Open Me Carefully.

**Other frequently cited poems**
Other clue poems include "Tell all the truth but tell it slant," which warns that "The Truth must dazzle gradually / Or every man be blind"; "There's a certain Slant of light," which "oppresses, like the Heft / Of Cathedral Tunes"; "The Soul selects her own Society," whose speaker is "Unmoved" by chariots and an emperor kneeling at her mat; "I like to see it lap the Miles," about a train; "I'm wife - I've finished that," which includes "I'm Czar"; and "Arcturus is his other name," which mocks a scientist who "Computes the stamens" of a flower and "has her in a class!"
